Jamal's first month at university in Manchester was the loneliest of his life. Rain, a single room, a kettle, and a flatmate he'd seen twice.
So when a friendly group at the student fair invited him to their Thursday dinners, he almost said yes on the spot. Free food, warm people, someone asking his name twice so they'd remember it.
Instead he went once, and on the second visit he asked the organiser, Hannah, some questions. 'Who pays for the dinners? Who runs it? What happens if someone stops coming?'
Hannah didn't blink. 'The student union gives us a small grant, it's on the website. A committee of five, elected each year. And people drop in and out all the time. No hard feelings.'
That evening he told Bilal on their weekly video call back home in Leeds. 'They answered everything,' he said. 'I'll keep going. But you're still my Sunday call, yeah?'

qa.q: Who did Jamal call every week?
qa.a: Jamal called Bilal on their weekly video call.

qa.q: Why did Jamal almost say yes on the spot?
qa.a: He felt very lonely in his first month, so warm people and free food were hard to resist.

qa.q: Which of Jamal's choices were wise, and why?
qa.a: He asked who pays, who runs it and what happens if you leave, and kept his weekly call with Bilal; open answers and outside friends protect against being drawn into an unhealthy group.

qa.q: How might Hannah see Jamal's questions?
qa.a: Hannah treats them as normal and reasonable, which is itself a good sign about the group.

grounding: It shows a lonely young man asking about a group's money, leadership and leaving, finding open answers, and keeping in touch with an outside friend.

The orientation hall of the engineering college still had banners from the freshers' welcome. Madhav, nineteen and far from home for the first time, had spent most evenings alone in his hostel room.
So when Shankar, a final-year student, invited him to a 'leadership fellowship', he went. The seniors were warm. They remembered his hometown. They offered to help with assignments.
At the second meeting, Madhav asked, 'Who funds this? Who's the head? And if I leave after a month, is that okay?'
The room went quiet. Shankar smiled, but his voice cooled. 'Those questions show a lack of trust, Madhav. The fellowship is for people who are all in.'
Madhav felt his face heat up. He said he'd think about it.
That night he knocked on the door of Vikas, his old school friend two floors down, and they walked to the canteen for chai. He didn't go to the third meeting.

qa.q: Who invited Madhav to the leadership fellowship?
qa.a: Shankar, a final-year student, invited him.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel when Shankar called his questions a lack of trust?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and uneasy, his face heating up, and sensed something was wrong.

qa.q: What did Madhav do well in dealing with the fellowship?
qa.a: He asked about money, leaders and leaving, read the cold reaction as a warning sign, and reconnected with an old friend instead of going back.

qa.q: How might Vikas see Madhav's late-night knock?
qa.a: Vikas may simply be glad to see an old friend, and that company gives Madhav a safe, ordinary place to belong.

grounding: It shows a lonely student asking about a group's funding, leaders and rules on leaving, and stepping back when questions are treated as disloyalty.

Dear Ritu,
Remember how lonely I sounded in my first month here? I've found a group: a community kitchen that cooks for construction workers on Sundays. They're warm, and I've started looking forward to weekends.
But I did what we promised each other before I left: I asked the boring questions. Who runs it? Where does the money come from? What happens if I want to stop?
Shobha didi, who coordinates, didn't blink. She showed me the donation register pinned on the wall, told me an elected committee changes every year, and said, "People come and go all the time. Come when you can." One volunteer left last month to focus on exams, and they threw her a small farewell.
That's when I relaxed. A group that was scared of questions would have got cross.
And I'm still calling you every Thursday, whatever happens. Tell me about your college fest.
Nazia

qa.a: On Sundays.

qa.q: What does Nazia mean by 'That's when I relaxed'?

qa.a: Ritu would likely feel relieved and proud that Nazia kept their promise and still makes time for her.

When I moved to Hyderabad, Reena, I didn't know a single soul. So when this "mentorship network" invited me to a Saturday meetup, I went. Free snacks, people clapping when I said my name. It felt amazing, honestly.
Third week, they asked me to sign up for the "inner programme". So I asked some basic things. Where does the fee go? Who is actually in charge? What if I want to quit halfway?
The mood changed. The organiser smiled and said, "Those questions come from fear, Ojas. Trust the process." Another guy said people who leave "always regret it". Nobody answered a single question.
That's when I stepped back. I went to the office cricket match that Sunday instead, and texted you that night, remember? A healthy group would have just answered. I'm still a bit lonely here, but I'd rather be lonely than trapped.

qa.q: What did the organiser say Ojas's questions came from?
qa.a: Those questions come from fear.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel when nobody answered the questions?
qa.a: Ojas felt uneasy and suspicious, sensing that warmth had turned to pressure once the questions started.

qa.q: What did Ojas do that a lonely newcomer could copy?
qa.a: Asked about fees, leaders and leaving before committing, and kept up outside ties like the office cricket and texting Reena.

qa.q: How might Reena have felt getting that text on Sunday night?
qa.a: Reena was probably glad to hear from Ojas, perhaps without realising how much that outside link mattered.

I share a PG room with Tanuja, so I noticed when she started going to the Sunday "purpose circle" at the community hall. She'd been low since her breakup; she came back from the first meeting humming.
The second week she dragged me along. After the talk she walked straight up to the organiser, Kunal, with a list on her phone. Who funds this? Who decides the rules? What happens to people who stop coming?
I was embarrassed; I thought he'd be offended. He wasn't. He showed her the accounts sheet, said there was a rotating committee, and added, "People leave all the time. Some come back. No hard feelings."
I don't know what she felt then. She looked calm. On the way home she said, "Okay. Maybe I'll keep going." Then she called her cousin and her old college gang to confirm their Thursday dinner, like always. She hasn't missed one.

Following Wednesday: on a video call, Afreen, his friend from college, asked who ran it. Vishal realised he didn't know. So at the next meet-up he asked the organiser three things: where the retreat fees went, who the leaders answered to, and what happened if someone wanted to stop coming. The organiser's smile tightened. "Those are outsider questions. Trust takes time."
Two Sundays later: Vishal compared that with the running club he had also joined, where the treasurer showed him the accounts and a member said, "Come when you like, skip when you like." He kept running on Sundays, and he kept calling Afreen.
